people.name: Woo Yee Sing
body: In 1883, Minneapolis was a young milling city, and Chinese food was new to it. That year, Woo Yee Sing and his brother Woo Du Sing opened the Canton Cafe, later known as John's Place. MNopedia identifies it as the first Chinese restaurant in Minneapolis.

Woo came to the United States at about 18. MNopedia says he arrived on the West Coast to severe anti-Chinese violence and moved to Minneapolis to leave it behind. Its own dates for that move vary, but by 1882 he was in the city. That same year Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, which suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years and barred courts from admitting Chinese immigrants to citizenship. Like many Chinese men at the time, MNopedia says, he ran a laundry before he went into the restaurant business.

In 1882, Westminster Presbyterian Church began offering English lessons for Chinese men, and Woo was one of the first students. In the summer of 1892, he married Liang May Seen in San Francisco, and she joined him in Minneapolis. In 1906, on a return visit to San Francisco, the couple adopted a son, Howard.

Their lives in Minnesota included open hostility. In 1912 a small bomb went off in the stairway leading to the restaurant, and his son later recalled being taunted with racist names. Woo died in 1925.
keyFacts: Immigrated to the U.S. at about 18.
1882: Among the first students in Westminster Presbyterian Church's English classes for Chinese men.
1883: Opened the Canton Cafe (later John's Place) with his brother Woo Du Sing, the first Chinese restaurant in Minneapolis.
1892: Married Liang May Seen. 1906: The couple adopted their son Howard.
1912: A small bomb exploded in the stairway to his restaurant.
1925: Died at about age 63.

people.name: Liang May Seen
body: On July 21, 1889, a young woman left the San Francisco brothel where she had been held, with help from the Presbyterian Mission Home. She lived at the Home for three years, where she converted to Christianity and studied English. In the summer of 1892, Liang May Seen married Woo Yee Sing and joined him in Minneapolis. MNopedia calls her the first Chinese woman to live in Minnesota. The National Park Service calls her the first to settle in Minneapolis.

Liang was born around 1871 in Kaiping District, Guangdong Province. At about 14, her parents sold her to a man who promised to arrange a wealthy marriage, and he sold her to a brothel owner in San Francisco's Chinatown.

In Minneapolis she built ties across the city. In 1904 she opened a Chinese curio shop, and many of the white women she befriended were its patrons. She formed friendships with white Minneapolis women, including the suffragist Mabeth Hurd Paige, whom she met through the Women's Foreign Missionary Society. In 1906 she and her husband adopted a son, Howard, in San Francisco. In 1920, when the church began English classes for women, she volunteered to teach them.
Liang lived to see the Chinese exclusion laws repealed in 1943, and she died in 1946. MNopedia says she was close to her niece, Margaret Woo Chinn.
keyFacts: About 1871: Born in Kaiping District, Guangdong, China.
1885: Sold at about age 14 and forced into a San Francisco brothel.
July 21, 1889: Reached the Presbyterian Mission Home.
Summer 1892: Married Woo Yee Sing and moved to Minneapolis.
1904: Opened a Chinese curio shop.
1920: Volunteered to teach English to women at the church.
1943: Chinese exclusion repealed. 1946: Died.

people.name: Walter James
body: For decades, people who worked or shopped in downtown Minneapolis knew the Nankin. Walter C. James opened it in 1919.

James was the oldest son of a Chinese family in Olympia, Washington, where his father worked in the oyster trade. In a 1970 interview he gave his birth year as 1891. The Chinese Heritage Foundation says 1892. At nine he went to his father's home village in Taishan, China, for about two and a half years. As a young man he worked in Tacoma, Seattle and Yakima, including as an interpreter for the U.S. Immigration Service. He moved to Chicago in 1913, soon left for Minneapolis, and opened the Canton restaurant before starting the Nankin.

He made the restaurant a meeting place. By the account of the Chinese American Association of Minnesota (CAAM), he and Stanley Chong turned part of the Nankin into clubrooms and worked with Westminster Presbyterian Church to offer language classes for immigrants. He joined the Twin Cities Rotary Club, the Heritage Foundation says as its first Chinese member, and raised funds for China during World War II.

Sources tell the founding of CAAM in different ways. The Minnesota Historical Society traces it to Chinese American Club gatherings at the Nankin in the 1930s and says the cafe's owner founded it in 1951. CAAM names that owner as James and credits him with founding the Chinese American Club in 1949, the same year, by one local history, that he sold the Nankin to the Golden and Chalfen families. CAAM also says he stayed involved until it was incorporated in 1967.

In 1970 he recorded an oral history, printed in 1995 in Chinese America: History & Perspectives, the journal of the Chinese Historical Society of America. CAAM and the Heritage Foundation give his death as 1973, and the journal's editors give 1976. He is buried at Lakewood Cemetery in Minneapolis.
keyFacts: 1891 or 1892: Born in Olympia, Washington.
1913: Moved to Chicago, then Minneapolis.
1919: Opened the Nankin.
1949: Sold the Minneapolis restaurant; CAAM dates his founding of the Chinese American Club to the same year.
1970: Recorded an oral history, printed in 1995.
2009: Named a Chinese Minnesotan of Note by the Chinese Heritage Foundation.

people.name: Chen Di
body: In the mid-1960s, a group of Chinese Americans working in Minnesota's professions and businesses decided the community should organize itself more formally. One of them was Di Chen, a research scientist at Honeywell. The Chinese American Association of Minnesota (CAAM) says he co-founded it in 1965. The University of Minnesota China Center, which writes his name as Chen Di, says he played a critical role in establishing the association in 1967. CAAM's history page gives two answers on its first president: its list of past presidents starts with Di Chen, for 1965 to 1967, and its text says Stanley Chong, a local businessman, was elected first president.

Chen was born in 1929 in Shixi, Zhejiang, and later moved to Taiwan. He graduated in electrical engineering from Taiwan University in 1952, came to the University of Minnesota in 1954 and earned a master's degree in 1956. After a doctorate at Stanford in 1959, he returned to teach at Minnesota until 1962, then spent about eighteen years at Honeywell Research.
CAAM says he died at his home in Mound, Minnesota, on October 14, 2019, at the age of 89.

1956: M.S., University of Minnesota. 1959: Doctorate, Stanford.
1962–1980: Honeywell Research.

1965–1967: First on CAAM's list of past presidents; its history text names Stanley Chong as first president.
October 14, 2019: Died at home in Mound, Minnesota, at 89.

people.name: Sping Lin
people.dates: born 1918, year of death not found
body: Sping Lin came to the University of Minnesota in the late 1940s to study insects and stayed for a career in brain chemistry. Born in 1918 in Zhongshan, Guangdong, he earned a bachelor's degree from Sun Yat-Sen University in 1940 and came to the United States in 1947. The University of Minnesota China Center says he chose Minnesota on the advice of Pu Zhelong, a doctoral student there.

He earned a master's degree in 1950 and a Ph.D. in 1952 in entomology. He stayed on as a research fellow in entomology and then in psychiatry and neurology, became an assistant professor in 1963 and an associate professor in 1969, and won grants from the National Institutes of Health.
In 2000 he and his wife, Ying-Ngoh, set up the Sping and Ying-Ngoh T. Lin Graduate Fellowship in entomology at the university. The China Center says it has supported six students since 2005.

1947: Came to the United States.
1952: Ph.D., University of Minnesota.
1969: Associate professor.
2000: Established a graduate fellowship with his wife, Ying-Ngoh.

people.name: Leeann Chin
body: Leeann Chin's restaurant business started with a thank-you. She worked as a seamstress in Minneapolis while raising five children, and she began cooking for her customers. They asked her to cater their parties and teach cooking classes. KSTP reports that investors in her catering business included Carl Pohlad, a past owner of the Minnesota Twins, and the actor Sean Connery.

Chin was born on February 13, 1933, in Guangzhou, China, where her father owned a grocery store. After marrying Tony Chin, she lived in Hong Kong for a few years. MPR News dates her arrival in Minnesota to 1957, after the end of Chinese exclusion.

In 1980 she opened the first Leeann Chin restaurant, at Bonaventure Mall in Minnetonka, which soon became a buffet. A second location opened in 1984 in St. Paul's train depot. In 1985 General Mills bought her name and restaurants. The business became independent again in the late 1980s, and she stayed involved until the late 1990s. The family sold the chain again in 2007.

Chin died in Seattle in March 2010, at 77. Her daughter Laura told MPR News that her mother's quick math would surprise the bankers. At the time the chain had more than 40 locations, mostly in the Twin Cities.
keyFacts: February 13, 1933: Born in Guangzhou, China; later lived in Hong Kong.
1957: Moved to Minnesota, by MPR's account.
1980: Opened the first Leeann Chin restaurant, Minnetonka.
1984: Second location in St. Paul's train depot.
1985: Sold her name and restaurants to General Mills; independent again in the late 1980s.
2007: Family sold the chain.
March 2010: Died in Seattle at 77.

people.name: Tony N. Leung
body: In 1994, Governor Arne Carlson appointed a Minneapolis lawyer to the state district court bench. With that appointment, Tony Leung became Minnesota's first Asian Pacific American judge. In 2011 he became a U.S. magistrate judge for the District of Minnesota, the state's first Asian Pacific American federal judge.

Leung was born in Hong Kong in 1959. His family immigrated in 1966, living first in Aurora, Illinois, and moving to Minneapolis a year later. His father, from a poor family in Taishan, China, cooked at the Minneapolis Nankin, and his mother cooked at the St. Paul Hilton. Later, though neither spoke English, they opened their own restaurant. Leung was co-valedictorian and student council president at his Minneapolis high school. At Yale he captained the Tae Kwon-do Club and won a bronze medal at the 1980 AAU Collegiate championships, and he earned a B.A. in political science. He took his law degree from New York University in 1985 and became an equity partner at Faegre & Benson.

Leung spent 31 years as a judge. Minnesota Lawyer says he handled high-profile cases, including excessive-force claims after the murder of George Floyd and criminal matters involving Derek Chauvin and Danny Heinrich, and that he settled hundreds of disputes as a mediator. He co-founded the Minnesota chapter of the National Asian Pacific American Bar Association and was the first chair of Twin Cities Diversity in Practice.
He retired from the federal bench in May 2025. Minnesota Lawyer reported in February 2026 that he is principal at LeungADR LLC, and it named him one of its 2025 Attorneys of the Year.
keyFacts: 1959: Born in Hong Kong. 1966: Family immigrated to the U.S.
Father a cook at the Nankin in Minneapolis.
1985: J.D., New York University School of Law.
1994: Appointed to the Minnesota district court, the state's first Asian Pacific American judge.
2011: Sworn in as a U.S. magistrate judge, the state's first Asian Pacific American federal judge.
May 2025: Retired from the federal bench.

people.name: Wong Kim Ark
people.dates: born 1871 or 1873, year of death unknown
body: In August 1895, a young cook arrived in San Francisco aboard the SS Coptic, coming home from a family visit in China. The port's Collector of Customs refused to let him in. Wong Kim Ark had been born in San Francisco, but customs officials argued that he was a Chinese subject because his parents were Chinese. He was held on ships for nearly five months while his case was tried, then released on bond.

Wong was born at 751 Sacramento Street in San Francisco's Chinatown, above a storefront owned by his merchant father. Sources give his birth year as 1871 or 1873. Under the Chinese Exclusion Act, his parents could not become U.S. citizens, and the government argued that their son could not be one either.

On March 28, 1898, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6–2 in United States v. Wong Kim Ark that, under the Fourteenth Amendment, a child born in the United States to parents settled here is a U.S. citizen. Justice Horace Gray wrote the majority opinion.

Wong worked as a cook for most of his documented life, and his citizenship was questioned again. On October 29, 1901, after a trip into Juárez, Mexico, he was arrested at El Paso, Texas. He was freed on a $300 bond, and on February 18, 1902, immigration officials accepted that he was the man whose citizenship the Court had upheld. He left for China in 1931, and there is no record of when he died.

The case still decides real disputes. On June 30, 2026, in Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court held that a 2025 executive order narrowing birthright citizenship was invalid. The Congressional Research Service reports that the majority read Wong Kim Ark as confirming that the Citizenship Clause covers nearly all children born in the United States.
keyFacts: 1871 or 1873: Born in San Francisco's Chinatown.
November 1894: Sailed to China to visit family.
August 1895: Denied reentry and held for nearly five months.
March 28, 1898: Supreme Court ruled 6–2 in his favor.
October 29, 1901: Arrested at El Paso. February 18, 1902: Officials accepted his identity.
1931: Left for China; no record of his death.
June 30, 2026: The Court relied on his case in Trump v. Barbara.

people.name: Mabel Ping-Hua Lee
body: On May 4, 1912, crowds lined the streets of New York for a huge parade demanding the vote for women. On horseback among its leaders was a Chinese teenager, Mabel Ping-Hua Lee. She was fighting for a vote she could not cast herself, because Chinese exclusion laws barred Chinese immigrants from becoming U.S. citizens.

Lee was born in Guangzhou, China, on October 7, in 1896 by the National Park Service's account and 1897 by the National Women's History Museum's. Her father, Dr. Lee Towe, was a Baptist missionary pastor who moved to the United States, and by 1905 she was enrolled at Erasmus Hall Academy in New York. She went on to Barnard College and then to Columbia University. In 1921 Columbia awarded her a Ph.D. in economics, making her the first Chinese woman in the United States to earn a doctorate in that field. Her dissertation was published as The Economic History of China.

When her father died in 1924, Lee took over leadership of the First Chinese Baptist Church in New York's Chinatown. She also founded the Chinese Christian Center, which offered English classes, vocational training, a kindergarten and a health clinic to Chinatown families.
Lee died in New York in 1966. In 2018 Congress designated the Chinatown post office at 6 Doyers Street as the Mabel Lee Memorial Post Office.

1905: Enrolled at Erasmus Hall Academy in New York.
May 4, 1912: On horseback, helped lead the New York suffrage parade.
1921: Ph.D. in economics, Columbia University.
1924: Took over leadership of the First Chinese Baptist Church.
2018: Congress named the 6 Doyers Street post office after her.

people.name: Chien-Shiung Wu
body: In late 1956, in a laboratory chilled to near absolute zero, a Columbia University physicist watched radioactive cobalt atoms decay. She was testing an idea most physicists assumed was settled: that nature makes no distinction between left and right, a principle called the conservation of parity. Chien-Shiung Wu's experiment showed that the principle does not hold in this kind of radioactive decay. Her colleagues Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang had proposed the theory, and they won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics. Wu did not share it.

Wu was born May 31, 1912, in Liuhe, a town in Taicang near Shanghai. Her father ran the Mingde School, which she attended. She graduated in physics from National Central University in Nanjing in 1934, moved to the United States in 1936 and earned her Ph.D. at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1940.

In 1943 she became the first female instructor in Princeton's physics department. In 1944 she joined Columbia University and the Manhattan Project, where she helped develop the gaseous diffusion process used to separate uranium isotopes. She became a U.S. citizen in 1954 and stayed at Columbia until she retired in 1981. Her 1965 book Beta Decay became a standard reference.

Wu received the National Medal of Science in 1975 and the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978. In 1975 she was elected the first woman president of the American Physical Society. She died in New York on February 16, 1997, and her ashes are buried at the Mingde School.
keyFacts: May 31, 1912: Born in Liuhe, Taicang, China.
1940: Ph.D., University of California, Berkeley.
1944: Joined Columbia University and the Manhattan Project.
1956–57: Her experiment overturned the conservation of parity in beta decay.
1975: National Medal of Science; first woman president of the American Physical Society.
February 16, 1997: Died in New York.

people.name: Anna May Wong
body: In 1922, a 17-year-old from Los Angeles starred in The Toll of the Sea, one of Hollywood's first Technicolor features. Anna May Wong, born Wong Liu Tsong on January 3, 1905, grew up working in her family's laundry. She started as a film extra in The Red Lantern (1919), and she became Hollywood's first Chinese American film star.

Stardom came with limits. Anti-miscegenation laws restricted her romantic leading roles, and she was usually cast as a villain, a victim or an exotic stereotype. Frustrated, she went to Europe, where she starred in Piccadilly (1929) and appeared on the London stage in The Circle of Chalk alongside the young Laurence Olivier. After returning, she appeared with Marlene Dietrich in Shanghai Express (1932). In 1935, MGM refused to consider her for O-Lan, the heroine of The Good Earth. The role went to a white actress, Luise Rainer, in yellowface. Rafu Shimpo calls it the most severe disappointment of her career.

In the 1950s she starred in The Gallery of Madame Liu-Tsong, which the National Women's History Museum describes as making her the first Asian American to lead a U.S. television show. On February 8, 1960, she received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. She died of a heart attack on February 3, 1961, at 56.
In 2022, she appeared on a quarter, the fifth coin in the U.S. Mint's American Women Quarters series.

1922: First leading role, in The Toll of the Sea.
1932: Shanghai Express, with Marlene Dietrich.
1935: MGM refused to consider her for The Good Earth.
1950s: The Gallery of Madame Liu-Tsong.
February 8, 1960: Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

people.name: I. M. Pei
body: When the plan for a glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre was unveiled in 1984, NBC News reports, many French people vehemently opposed it. It was finished in 1989 and is now one of the most recognizable entrances in the world. Its architect, Ieoh Ming Pei, had already reshaped American cities.

Pei was born April 26, 1917, in Guangzhou, China. In 1935 he sailed to San Francisco to study architecture, intending to go home to practice; World War II and the revolution in China prevented his return. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania and then at MIT, where he earned a bachelor's degree in 1940, and he took his master's at Harvard's Graduate School of Design in 1946.

In 1955 he founded I. M. Pei & Associates. His American works include the Mesa Laboratory of the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colorado (1967), the East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. (1978), and the John F. Kennedy Library near Boston (1979). Abroad, he designed the Fragrant Hill Hotel near Beijing (1982) and the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong (1989).
In 1983 he won the Pritzker Architecture Prize. He died in May 2019, at 102.

people.name: Maya Lin
body: In 1981, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund held an open, blind competition to design a memorial in Washington, D.C. The jury reviewed 1,420 entries and chose one unanimously. Its designer was Maya Lin, a 21-year-old Yale undergraduate, who had developed the design as an assignment for a college architecture class. It is a low wall of black granite cut into the earth and carved with the names of the dead, dedicated on November 13, 1982.

Lin was born in Ohio on October 5, 1959, and raised in Athens, Ohio. Both her parents had left China around 1949. Her father, a ceramic artist, became dean of fine arts at Ohio University. Her mother, Julia Chang Lin, came on a Smith College scholarship and became a poet and literature professor there. Her brother, Tan Lin, became a poet.

At Yale, Lin moved from zoology to architecture. She went on to design the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama (1989), and The Women's Table at Yale (1993). Since 2001 she has worked on the Confluence Project, a collaboration with Columbia River tribes and river communities in Washington and Oregon. Her environmental work includes Wave Fields, Ghost Forest in New York's Madison Square Park (2021), and What Is Missing?, which she calls her final memorial. She also designed the 2009 home of the Museum of Chinese in America.
Lin received the National Medal of Arts in 2009 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

1981: Won the Vietnam Veterans Memorial competition at 21, from 1,420 entries.
November 13, 1982: Memorial dedicated.
1989: Civil Rights Memorial, Montgomery, Alabama.
2009: National Medal of Arts.
2016: Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: Amy Tan
body: In the 1980s, a freelance business writer in California was producing speeches for corporate executives, sometimes under names that did not sound Chinese. At 33, she started writing fiction about Chinese mothers and their American-born daughters. Those stories became The Joy Luck Club. G.P. Putnam's Sons gave her a $50,000 advance, and she quit business writing to finish the book. When it came out in 1989 it was a finalist for both the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award. In 1993 it became a film directed by Wayne Wang, with Tan and Ronald Bass as screenwriters.

Amy Tan was born on February 19, 1952, in Oakland, California. Her parents, John and Daisy Tan, were Chinese immigrants, and the family spoke English, Mandarin, Cantonese and Shanghainese. When she was 15, her father, an electrical engineer and Baptist minister, and her older brother both died of brain tumors, within a year of each other. She finished high school in Montreux, Switzerland, and earned bachelor's and master's degrees in English and linguistics from San José State University.

Tan went on to write The Kitchen God's Wife (1991), The Hundred Secret Senses (1995), The Bonesetter's Daughter (2001), Saving Fish from Drowning (2005) and The Valley of Amazement (2013). She also wrote children's books, memoirs including Where the Past Begins, and an opera libretto. The Backyard Bird Chronicles gathers her bird observations.
The National Endowment for the Humanities lists her as a 2021 National Humanities Medal recipient, "for expanding the American literary canon."
keyFacts: February 19, 1952: Born in Oakland, California, to Chinese immigrant parents.
At 33: Began writing fiction while working as a business writer.
1989: The Joy Luck Club published.
1993: Film directed by Wayne Wang.

people.name: Yo-Yo Ma
body: At age four, a small boy in Paris began studying the cello with his father. That boy, Yo-Yo Ma, became one of the best-known classical musicians in the world.

Ma was born on October 7, 1955, in Paris to Chinese parents: his father, Hiao-Tsiun Ma, was a violinist, composer and music teacher, and his mother, Marina, was a mezzo-soprano. When he was around seven the family moved to New York City, where he continued his studies at the Juilliard School. In 1963 he performed on national television at a Washington fundraiser for the future Kennedy Center. He graduated from New York's Professional Children's School in 1970 and earned a liberal arts degree from Harvard in 1976.

In 1998 he founded what is now Silkroad, a collective of musicians from many countries, named for the ancient trade routes linking China, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silkroad describes its mission as "radical cultural collaboration."

The Carnegie Foundation counts more than 100 albums and 18 Grammy Awards, and his official biography gives higher figures. He has received the Kennedy Center Honors, the National Medal of Arts and the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and he has taken Bach's six suites for solo cello on a tour of six continents. Since 2006 he has served as a United Nations Messenger of Peace.
keyFacts: October 7, 1955: Born in Paris to Chinese parents.
Around age 7: Moved with his family to New York City.
1963: Televised performance at a Kennedy Center fundraiser.
1976: Liberal arts degree, Harvard.
1998: Founded Silkroad.
2010: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
people.connectToWork: How does your intake handle someone whose birthplace, citizenship and heritage all point in different directions, and what would you ask instead of guessing?

people.name: Michelle Kwan
body: Michelle Kwan won 43 championships, including five world titles and nine U.S. national titles, plus two Olympic medals. By the Americas Society's account, she holds the record for the most titles of any U.S. figure skater.

Kwan was born on July 7, 1980, in Torrance, California, to Danny and Estella Kwan, who had moved from Hong Kong to California. She won Olympic silver at the 1998 Nagano Games and bronze at the 2002 Salt Lake City Games, and she entered the U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Hall of Fame in 2022.

Her second career was in diplomacy. In 2006 the State Department named her its first public diplomacy envoy, and for about a decade she traveled abroad meeting young people. She also served as a senior advisor in the department's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs. She earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Denver and a master's degree from Tufts University's Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy.

The Senate confirmed her as U.S. ambassador to Belize on September 29, 2022. She was the first U.S. ambassador there since 2017 and the first Asian American woman in the post. Her service ended in January 2025.
keyFacts: July 7, 1980: Born in Torrance, California, to parents from Hong Kong.
Five world titles and nine U.S. titles; 43 championships in all.
Silver, 1998 Nagano. Bronze, 2002 Salt Lake City.
2006: Named the State Department's first public diplomacy envoy.
September 29, 2022: Confirmed as ambassador to Belize; served until January 2025.

people.name: Gary Locke
body: Gary Locke spent his early childhood in Yesler Terrace, a Seattle public housing complex, and spoke only Chinese until kindergarten. Decades later he became the first Chinese American to serve as U.S. ambassador to China.

Locke was born on January 21, 1950, in Seattle, the second of five children of James and Julie Locke. His father was brought to the United States from China in 1921 and served in World War II with the 5th Armored Division from Normandy to Berlin. His mother was born in Hong Kong. The family ran a restaurant on Post Alley in Pike Place Market. Locke graduated from Yale in 1972 and from Boston University School of Law in 1975.

He worked as a King County prosecutor, was elected to the Washington House of Representatives in 1982, and in 1993 was elected King County executive. In 1996 Washington voters elected him the first Chinese American governor in U.S. history. He served from 1997 to 2005. In 2003 he gave the Democratic response to the State of the Union address.

In 2009 he became Secretary of Commerce, the first Chinese American in that role, and from 2011 to 2014 he was ambassador to China. He has also chaired the board of the Committee of 100 and served as interim president of Bellevue College. As of October 2026 Dorsey & Whitney lists him as a senior advisor.
keyFacts: January 21, 1950: Born in Seattle.
1972: B.A., Yale. 1975: J.D., Boston University.
1997–2005: Governor of Washington.
2009–2011: U.S. Secretary of Commerce.
2011–2014: U.S. ambassador to China.
Later: Chair of the Committee of 100 board; interim president of Bellevue College.

people.name: Alice Wong
body: In 2014 Alice Wong founded the Disability Visibility Project, which began as an oral history partnership with StoryCorps to collect disabled people's own stories. It grew into a podcast and a series of books. She described herself as a disabled activist, writer, editor and community organizer.

Wong was born in 1974 near Indianapolis, Indiana, to parents who had immigrated from Hong Kong. She was diagnosed with muscular dystrophy at birth, and KQED reports that doctors told her parents she would not live to 18. She used a power wheelchair and, later, a tracheostomy to breathe. She earned a bachelor's degree at Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis and a master's at UC San Francisco, and she worked at UCSF as a staff research associate for more than ten years.

From 2013 to 2015 she served on the National Council on Disability, at President Obama's request. In 2016 she co-founded #CripTheVote. She edited Disability Visibility: First-Person Stories from the Twenty-First Century (2020) and Disability Intimacy (2024) and wrote a memoir, Year of the Tiger: An Activist's Life (2022). Its publisher's description ties the title to the tiger's place in Chinese culture. She was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2024.
She died of an infection at the UCSF hospital on November 14, 2025, at age 51.
keyFacts: 1974: Born near Indianapolis to parents from Hong Kong.
2013–2015: Member of the National Council on Disability.
2014: Founded the Disability Visibility Project.
2020: Disability Visibility anthology.
2022: Year of the Tiger memoir.
2024: MacArthur Fellow.
November 14, 2025: Died in San Francisco, age 51.

people.name: Anna Wang
body: Anna Wang, a former electrical engineer in California, and her husband Albert Wang, a doctor, could not find services that fit their son after he was diagnosed with autism in the early 1990s. The Wangs and other Chinese American families began meeting to support each other, and in 1996 they launched Friends of Children with Special Needs (FCSN).

Accounts of the start differ in emphasis. A 2016 Lucile Packard Foundation article describes the Wangs and nine other families launching the group. FCSN's own history credits a special education teacher, Shiow-Luan Chen, and a parent, Linmei Chiao, with bringing families together for the first meeting, and it says Anna Wang started the Milpitas Playgroup in 1998, along with job training projects later on. In the 2016 article she spoke of a community culture in which parents talked about children admitted to top universities and never about a child with a disability, and she described parents who had hidden their children.
The Alameda County Women's Hall of Fame inducted her in 2023 for community service and listed her as FCSN's co-founder and vice president.
keyFacts: 1996: FCSN launched with Albert Wang and other families.
1998: Started the Milpitas Playgroup.
2016: Vice president of community relations and enrichment programs at FCSN.
2023: Alameda County Women's Hall of Fame.

institutions.name: Chinese American Association of Minnesota
body: The Minnesota Historical Society calls the Chinese American Association of Minnesota (CAAM) the oldest and largest Chinese American community organization in the state. It traces CAAM to Chinese American Club gatherings at the Nankin Cafe in the 1930s and says the cafe's owner founded it in 1951 and helped incorporate it in 1967. CAAM names that owner as Walter James. Its history page lists six founding members in 1967 and gives two answers on its first president: its list of past presidents starts with Di Chen, for 1965 to 1967, then Stanley Chong, for 1967 to 1968, and its text says Stanley Chong was elected first president. CAAM's page on Di Chen says he co-founded the association in 1965. The University of Minnesota China Center dates his role in establishing it to 1967.

CAAM describes its goal as promoting the cultural heritage and enhancing the quality of life of Chinese Americans in Minnesota. It says it is politically neutral. Today it runs the Twin Cities Chinese Language School and the CAAM Chinese Dance Theater, the Stanley and Marvel Chong Scholarship, English and after-school programs, a Pre-Thanksgiving Free Lunch at Dorothy Day Place, a Chinese Cafe at IFest-MN and a Heritage Music Project. It posted about its grand gala in July 2026. Its newsletter, News & Views, ran from 1997 to 2003 by CAAM's own count.
keyFacts: 1930s: Chinese American Club gatherings at the Nankin Cafe.
1951: Founded, by MNHS and CAAM.
1965: Di Chen co-founded it, by CAAM's page on him; the China Center dates his role to 1967.
1965–1967: Di Chen, first on CAAM's list of past presidents; its history text names Stanley Chong as first president.
1967: Incorporated.

institutions.name: Chinese Social Service Center
body: The Chinese Social Service Center (CSSC) describes itself as a bridge between American mainstream society and the Chinese community in the Twin Cities. The United Way 211 listing, last verified November 20, 2025, lists counseling and support for new immigrants, ESL and citizenship classes, help applying for Social Security, SSI, Medicare, Medical Assistance, MinnesotaCare, housing and WIC, translation, transportation, youth programs, a senior program, and homemaking and PCA home care for older adults and people with disabilities, contracted with Medica.

Its status as a nonprofit is in doubt. ProPublica shows its latest return as a Form 990-EZ for fiscal 2021, filed in December 2022, and says it is not on the IRS's most recent list of tax-exempt organizations. Call before you refer anyone.
keyFacts: Listed services include home care, translation, and help with Medicare and Medical Assistance.
211 listing last verified November 20, 2025.

institutions.name: Museum of Chinese in America
body: The Museum of Chinese in America (MOCA) began in 1980 as the New York Chinatown History Project, founded by John Kuo Wei Tchen and Charlie Lai. In 1984 it moved into four second-floor rooms at 70 Mulberry Street and presented its first exhibition, Eight Pound Livelihood, about Chinese laundrymen in New York. It took its current name in 2007, and in 2009 it moved to 215 Centre Street, in a space redesigned by Maya Lin.

On January 23, 2020, a fire tore through 70 Mulberry Street, where its collection of more than 85,000 artifacts was housed. Much of the collection turned out to be salvageable. On January 10, 2024, MOCA bought its Centre Street building for $51.1 million with a $39.4 million mortgage from New York City. Our Town Downtown reported protests by some Chinatown activists, who accused the museum's leaders of selling out the neighborhood.
keyFacts: 1980: Founded as the New York Chinatown History Project.
1984: First exhibition, Eight Pound Livelihood.
2009: Moved to 215 Centre Street.
January 23, 2020: Fire at 70 Mulberry Street.
January 10, 2024: Bought its Centre Street building.

institutions.name: Chinese Historical Society of America
body: In 1963, five community members in San Francisco's Chinatown, Thomas W. Chinn, C.H. Kwock, Chingwah Lee, H.K. Wong and Thomas W.S. Wu, founded the Chinese Historical Society of America to document the history of Chinese people in the United States. The society says fewer than 250,000 people of Chinese descent lived in the country at the time.

Since 2001 it has been housed in the former Chinatown YWCA at 965 Clay Street, a landmark building designed by Julia Morgan. Its journal, Chinese America: History & Perspectives, printed the oral history of Walter James, founder of Minneapolis's Nankin Cafe, in 1995.
keyFacts: 1963: Founded in San Francisco.
2001: Moved into the former Chinatown YWCA.
Publishes Chinese America: History & Perspectives.

institutions.name: Friends of Children with Special Needs
body: FCSN says ten families of children with special needs formed it in 1996. Its own history dates the first meeting to April 4, 1996, in Saratoga, and says it took its current name at the end of that year. A 2016 Lucile Packard Foundation article describes Chinese American families who could not find services that understood the immigrant experience, and a housing complex with 10 four-bedroom units for adults, owned by 26 FCSN families.

It opened its 6,000-square-foot Fremont center in 2006 and a San Jose center in 2017. Its website lists adult day, supported and independent living, supported employment, after-school, respite, family outreach and summer camp programs, and it marked its 30th anniversary on June 6, 2026. It is in California, not Minnesota, and appears here as one example of a family-run service.
keyFacts: April 4, 1996: First meeting, Saratoga.
2006: Fremont center opened.
2017: San Jose center opened.
June 6, 2026: 30th-anniversary Family Day.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Chinese means people who trace family to China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Southeast Asia or elsewhere, from families here for generations to recent immigrants and students. They speak Mandarin, Cantonese, Toisanese, other languages or only English, and follow many faiths or none. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Chinese Minnesotans understand disability. The research below is small, mostly qualitative, often about autism or mental illness, and some of it is about China rather than the U.S.
questions: How do you and your family understand what's going on? What words do you use for it, in English and in Chinese?
Who gave you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped, or has it got in the way?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Which language and dialect do you prefer, spoken and written? Do you read Simplified or Traditional characters?
Would you like a professional interpreter, so that family members do not have to interpret?
Who do you want involved in decisions, and who would you rather not have involved?
What information would help you most about eligibility, your rights, and what happens to your personal information?
Who helps with care now, and how is that going for them? Would a break or other support help?
Would you like to connect with other Chinese-speaking families or a community group, or would you rather keep this private?
Some families also use other kinds of care. Is there anything you use that we should know about or plan around?
If you want to share it, what do you think led to this? You do not have to answer.
What does a good life look like to you, apart from school or career?

context.heading: What studies and reviews report about explanations and stigma
body: A 2007 literature review by Chiang and Hadadian reports older findings that the birth of a disabled child may be taken as evidence of a parent's bad karma or a curse from ancestors, that some mothers blamed themselves for breaking pregnancy taboos, and that families often kept a disability secret and may have avoided outside help. It is a review of older work, not a new study, and it describes no particular family.

In a study of 10 Chinese American parents of autistic children, Yang and Crehan (2023) found that cultural stigma shaped how parents understood the diagnosis. The authors propose that experiences both before and after immigration shape parenting attitudes, so views can differ by generation, place of origin and time in the U.S. They recommend culturally sensitive education materials.

A 2025 interview study of 20 Asian American veterans who had experienced suicidal thoughts, from many ethnic backgrounds and mostly men, found that shame and stigma discouraged disclosure and help-seeking. It does not report on Chinese Americans separately.

sources.label: Chiang and Hadadian, International Journal of Special Education (2007)
Yang and Crehan, Autism & Developmental Language Impairments (2023)
Krishnamurti and colleagues, Frontiers in Psychiatry (2025)

context.heading: Family, caregiving and who decides
body: In a focus-group study, Han, Diwan and Sun (2019) compared 30 Chinese American and 27 European American family caregivers of people with mental illness. Caregivers in both groups described heavy emotional and health strain. The Chinese American caregivers more often described shame, a lack of information and being protective of their relative, and the European American caregivers stressed advocating for their relative. The sample is small, and it does not predict any one caregiver.
Do not assume who decides. The person, a parent, a spouse, an adult child or a grandparent may each have a part, and the disabled person's own voice comes first even if a relative speaks first.

sources.label: Han, Diwan and Sun, Transcultural Psychiatry (2019)

context.heading: Words, language and format
body: Zhong (2020) traces three Mandarin terms in China. 残废 (cánfèi), glossed as disabled and wasted, was in use before 1984 and went with keeping people out of public view. 残疾 (cánjí) is a medical framing, glossed as disabled and diseased. 残障 (cánzhàng) points to barriers in social systems. That essay is about China. Usage in Cantonese, in Taiwan and among U.S.-born Chinese Americans may differ, so ask which words the person uses, avoid 残废, and describe the specific support when you are unsure.

Ask about spoken language and written characters separately. Use a trained professional interpreter rather than a child or relative, especially when a diagnosis is being discussed. In English, follow what the person uses. Alice Wong, profiled on this page, called herself a disabled activist.

sources.label: Zhong, China Development Brief (2020)
Disability Visibility Project, About

context.heading: Families who organized, and what they say helped
body: Friends of Children with Special Needs in California is one documented example of Chinese American families building their own services. The 2016 Lucile Packard Foundation article describes peer support from other families, services in families' own languages, and parent training on IEPs and other systems. It also describes parents who had hidden their children and a culture of celebrating academic success while staying silent about disability. It is one article about one organization, and it does not tell you what any family in Minnesota wants or knows.

sources.label: Liu, Lucile Packard Foundation for Children's Health, "Celebrating 20 Years Serving the Chinese American Special Needs Community" (2016)
Friends of Children with Special Needs, History and Achievement

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no Minnesota research on Chinese American families and disability, and no U.S. research on how traditional Chinese medicine, acupuncture or faith practices are used alongside disability services. We did not find a Chinese disability-specific group or a disability self-advocate of Chinese heritage based in Minnesota, though the search was limited. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

organizations.intro: The Minnesota Historical Society traces organized Chinese American community life in the state to club gatherings at the Nankin Cafe in the 1930s. Today's groups include cultural associations, weekend language schools, dance and arts groups, a church with services in three languages, and a philanthropic foundation. We did not find a Chinese-language newspaper or radio program based in Minnesota, or a reputable source naming a Minnesota WeChat account, so ask local partners where people get news. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. These are starting points for learning.

entries.name: Twin Cities Chinese Language School
entries.purpose: Founded in 1976 and run with CAAM. Weekend Chinese language and culture classes using Traditional characters, with lion dance, dragon dance and crafts. Its calendar runs through December 2026.

entries.name: CAAM Chinese Dance Theater
entries.purpose: Year-round Chinese dance training for all ages, summer camps, residencies and an annual production at The O'Shaughnessy. Its 2026 production ran January 17 and 18.

entries.name: Chinese Heritage Foundation
entries.purpose: Established in 2004 with The Minneapolis Foundation to build understanding of Chinese history and culture among Minnesotans, largely through grants. Its programs include fellowships, opera projects and Chinese Minnesotans of Note. Its founder, Ming Li Tchou, died in 2024.

entries.name: Twin City Chinese Christian Church
entries.purpose: A church with Sunday services in Cantonese, English and Mandarin, plus fellowships, youth and children's programs, and a Sunday shuttle.

entries.name: Minnesota Yucai Chinese School
entries.location: West metro; classes in Plymouth and online
entries.purpose: A nonprofit founded in 2007. Offers online Saturday Chinese classes, math and reading enrichment, SAT and ACT preparation and a summer camp, with a 2026–2027 class schedule posted.

entries.name: Minnesota China Friendship Garden Society
entries.purpose: Runs the free public St. Paul–Changsha China Friendship Garden with St. Paul Parks and Recreation, including a Hmong Cultural Plaza. Held a Peony Festival in May 2026.

entries.name: Alliance of Minnesota Chinese Organizations
entries.purpose: Received a $30,000 Arts & Cultural Heritage Fund grant in fiscal 2024 for Asian music and dance events. That grant record, running to January 2025, is the latest we found, and we found no website.

entries.name: University of Minnesota Chinese student groups
entries.purpose: The university's China Center lists Chinese Students and Scholars Services, China Global Connection, the Chinese Student Union and the Chinese American Student Association.
entries.linkLabel: University of Minnesota China Center list

entries.name: China Insight
entries.purpose: Meet Minneapolis lists it as a monthly English-language paper on Chinese and American cultures and business. We could not confirm recent issues, because its site would not load for us.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota immigrants and communities of color. Multicultural, not specific to Chinese Minnesotans.

entries.name: OCA – Asian Pacific American Advocates
entries.purpose: Works through local chapters on civic participation and access to resources. Its chapter list shows no Minnesota chapter. The nearest are in Wisconsin, Illinois, Michigan and Missouri.

entries.name: Committee of 100
entries.purpose: Established in 1990. Publishes the State of Chinese Americans survey and works on full participation of Chinese Americans and U.S.–Greater China ties.

entries.name: Chinese American Citizens Alliance
entries.purpose: Says it has advocated for Chinese Americans since 1895. We found no Minnesota lodge.

entries.name: Chinese for Affirmative Action
entries.purpose: Works on immigrant rights, language diversity, education equity, economic justice, Chinese-language digital engagement and community safety. It features Stop AAPI Hate among its work.

entries.name: National Asian Pacific Center on Aging
entries.purpose: Advocates for Asian American and Pacific Islander older adults and runs a helpline for benefits questions, with Mandarin and Cantonese lines.

entries.name: Stop AAPI Hate
entries.purpose: Collects reports of anti-Asian hate and publishes research. Its form is available in 21 languages, including Traditional and Simplified Chinese.

entries.name: World Journal
entries.purpose: Chinese-language news site in Traditional characters, 世界新聞網.

entries.name: Sing Tao Daily, U.S. edition
entries.purpose: U.S., China, Hong Kong and Taiwan news in Traditional characters, 星島日報, with immigration and housing sections.

entries.name: NBC Asian America
entries.purpose: A section of NBC News on Asian American culture and politics.

entries.name: AsAmNews
entries.purpose: A daily digital news site on Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, published by the nonprofit Asian American Media Inc.

entries.name: China Press
entries.purpose: A U.S. daily founded in 1990, 侨报, with a web platform in Simplified and Traditional characters. A 2018 Hoover Institution report calls it the flagship pro-PRC newspaper in the U.S. and says a Chinese government office appears to control its parent group.

entries.name: SinoVision
entries.purpose: A Chinese-language broadcaster, 美国中文电视, that its app listing says began in 1990. The 2018 Hoover report places it in the same group as the China Press. NTD, an outlet critical of the Chinese government, reported in 2024 that its TV channel would end that August. Its app was last updated in August 2025.
